# jellyfin_plugin (Resource)

Installs a plugin on the Jellyfin server. The server may require a restart after installation.

Jellyfin's *Update Plugins* scheduled task (key `PluginUpdates`) upgrades every plugin to the newest compatible version its repositories offer, at startup and every 24 hours by default. This resource counts automatic plugin updates as on while that task has at least one trigger in `GET /ScheduledTasks`, and as off while it has none or the server lists no such task. The setting is global: the `autoUpdate` flag in a plugin's `meta.json` is not read. While updates are on, `version` is a minimum that any installed version at least as new satisfies, so a plugin the task upgraded stays as it is; while they are off, `version` is exact, and the next apply reinstalls the configured version in place of any other. To hold every plugin at its configured version, remove the task's triggers with `jellyfin_scheduled_task`; with the `depends_on` below, the apply that removes them also reinstalls each plugin the task had moved past its `version`.

When a `jellyfin_scheduled_task` in the configuration manages `PluginUpdates`, give every `jellyfin_plugin` `depends_on = [jellyfin_scheduled_task.<name>]`, or give the module that holds the plugins a `depends_on` on it. Terraform then plans and applies the schedule before the plugins, so each plugin is planned against the schedule the apply sets, and a `jellyfin_restart` that depends on the plugins restarts the server only after the schedule is written. Without it, Terraform may refresh a plugin before it plans the task; if the task changes whether updates are on and that changes the plugin's plan, the plan fails with an error asking for `depends_on`, `terraform destroy` included, and even a plan that succeeds may apply the schedule after the plugins. A plan that replaces the plugin for a new `name` or `repository_url` is the same under either schedule and does not fail, but the provider cannot see a replacement that `-replace` asks for, so such a plan can still fail this way; `depends_on` avoids it. A tainted plugin is planned as a new one, so it does not fail. If the task resource depends on a plugin, as a `for_each` over tasks that plugins add can, manage `PluginUpdates` in a `jellyfin_scheduled_task` of its own. With `depends_on`, triggers unknown until apply count as on; without it, a plugin planned before the task uses the schedule the server has. Either way, a plugin whose plan depends on the schedule gets a warning naming the schedule it was planned with, and if the apply sets the other one, the next plan corrects it. A plan that does not refresh the plugin, such as with `-refresh=false`, uses whether updates were on when Terraform last refreshed or created it, or off while its state, written by an earlier provider version, has not been refreshed since, with a warning when the configuration changes that. Only resources that use the same provider configuration see each other's plans: across provider configurations, even with `depends_on`, a plugin is planned against the schedule the server has, without a warning or an error, and the next plan corrects it, so keep the task and the plugins on one provider alias.

Replacing the resource also replaces the resources that take its `id`, such as `jellyfin_plugin_configuration`, because the `id` is unknown until the plugin is installed again. They then write their configuration again, which Jellyfin accepts only once a restart has loaded the reinstalled plugin, so put a `jellyfin_restart` between them, as the `jellyfin_security_plugin_configuration` example does.

## Example Usage

```terraform
resource "jellyfin_plugin" "example" {
  name           = "Bookshelf"
  version        = "13.0.0.0"
  repository_url = "https://repo.jellyfin.org/files/plugin/manifest.json"

  # The Update Plugins schedule decides whether version is a minimum or exact,
  # so Terraform must plan and apply it before the plugin.
  depends_on = [jellyfin_scheduled_task.plugin_updates]
}

# Jellyfin's Update Plugins task upgrades every plugin at startup and daily.
# While it has triggers, version is a minimum, and Bookshelf may run a newer
# release without Terraform reinstalling 13.0.0.0. Without triggers the task
# never runs, which stops automatic updates for every plugin and holds
# Bookshelf at exactly 13.0.0.0.
resource "jellyfin_scheduled_task" "plugin_updates" {
  key      = "PluginUpdates"
  triggers = []
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) The plugin package name. Used as the import key (e.g. `terraform import jellyfin_plugin.x "SSO-Auth"`).

### Optional

- `repository_url` (String) The repository URL from which to install the plugin. Required when creating the resource and resolved automatically on import when the exact package version is still available.
- `version` (String) The plugin version to install, as the repository lists it (e.g. `13.0.0.0`), or a keyword: `latest` installs the newest version the repositories offer, and `supported` installs the Jellyfin Security release this provider was tested against, in the build the server accepts. A keyword is resolved only when the plugin is installed, or when it replaces another value, and stays in state as written; `installed_version` holds the result. Omitted, it installs as `supported` does for Jellyfin Security and as `latest` does for any other plugin, and then holds the installed version, as it also does once a keyword is removed from the configuration. A configured version is a minimum while Jellyfin's automatic plugin updates are on, meaning its `PluginUpdates` task (*Update Plugins*) has at least one trigger, and exact while they are off. A keyword is compared the same way, as the version it resolves to, only when the plugin is installed or when the keyword replaces another value; kept in the configuration, it follows whatever version is installed, under either schedule. As a minimum, any installed version at least as new satisfies it: `version` keeps the configured value while `installed_version` follows the updates, creating the resource adopts an installed version newer than it instead of installing an older one, unless Jellyfin lists that version as `NotSupported` or `Malfunctioned`, and changing the value reinstalls the plugin only when the installed version is older than the new value. As exact, an installed version other than the configured one reads back into `version`, so the next apply reinstalls the configured version, and changing the value reinstalls the plugin unless the new value names the installed version, as a keyword set on an imported plugin usually does. A change that needs no reinstall only changes state; a reinstall replaces the resource. A refresh cannot see the configuration, so the provider stores whether it sets `version` whenever an apply creates or changes the resource, and until then, as after an import or in state an earlier provider version wrote, counts a version in state as set. The first plan after the task upgrades the plugin therefore changes `version` in place once, only in state, in two cases: where the configuration omits `version` for a plugin imported without it, created by an earlier provider version, or whose `version` was removed from the configuration while it named the installed version, `version` moves to the new installed version; and where a configuration adds a `version` equal to the one in state, `version` moves from the installed version back to the configured one.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) The plugin ID assigned by Jellyfin after installation.
- `installed_version` (String) The version Jellyfin lists for the plugin, which can be newer than `version` while Jellyfin's automatic plugin updates are on. While an update waits for a restart Jellyfin lists both versions, and this keeps the one it held before, whose `status` then reads `Superceded` or `Superseded`.
- `status` (String) The status Jellyfin lists for `installed_version`: `Active` once it is loaded; `Restart` while it waits for a restart to load, as a new install or update does; `Superceded` or `Superseded`, depending on the Jellyfin version, while a newer version installed next to it waits for a restart to replace it; `Disabled` while it is disabled on the Plugins page of the Jellyfin dashboard; `NotSupported` while it targets a Jellyfin version other than the server's, as after a Jellyfin upgrade, so Jellyfin does not load it; or `Malfunctioned` once it has failed to load, which the server log explains. A version Jellyfin removes at the next restart (`Deleted`) is never read. Creating the resource never keeps or adopts a version Jellyfin lists as `NotSupported` or `Malfunctioned`: it installs the configured version instead, which fails, naming the version, while no enabled repository offers a build of it for this server. It also fails when Jellyfin lists the version it installed as `NotSupported` or `Malfunctioned`; Terraform then keeps the plugin as tainted, and the next apply installs the configured version again, after uninstalling this one unless the resource sets `create_before_destroy`. Each refresh reads the status, and an update in place keeps it.

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
terraform import jellyfin_plugin.example "<plugin-name>"
```
